releases.title: Mountains shaped by erosion, and textures that stop jumping
releases.summary: Mountain ranges before about 65 million years ago, and the ranges the future's collisions build, are now carved by a model of rivers eroding rising rock -- valley networks that branch, divides that sit off-centre toward the thrust front, massifs and passes along the crest -- tuned against the real ranges of today until a blurred-and-regrown Himalaya, Alps and Andes looked like the originals. And a long-standing fault that made every ground texture jump at each 5-million-year step is fixed.

sections.name: Mountains
items: The Caledonides, the Appalachian and Variscan belts, the Urals, the Central Pangean Mountains, the Gondwanan and Precambrian belts, and the future's collision ranges are eroded into real mountain form: dendritic valleys, spurs, plateaus that stay calm, and a steep front with a longer back slope instead of a symmetric tent.
The relief is matched to what real ranges of the same height and steepness carry, including their few deep gorges and high crests, so it is neither smoother nor lumpier than the Earth's.
Ranges carry rock bands along their length, so they break into parallel ridges and long valleys the way folded belts do, not only into valleys running down their flanks.
The future's ranges no longer carry the extra-deep synthetic valleys that made them look lumpy; they are eroded like the rest, and their highest ground stops near seven kilometres.
Today's mountains, and the Cenozoic's, are untouched: their relief is the real terrain's.
Ice sheets in past glaciations bury their mountains smoothly, as a kilometre of ice does, with the ranges showing through only near the margins.

sections.name: Motion
items: Ground textures -- mountain valleys, rock and soil tints, fine relief -- used to jump every 5 million years, by hundreds of kilometres in deep time, because the rotation that keeps them on their plate was applied about the wrong axis. They now ride their crust smoothly through each step, and the valleys themselves persist from one step to the next.

releases.title: Mountains that are ranges: valleys, massifs and passes in deep time, and chains in the future
releases.summary: The Palaeozoic and Precambrian ranges read as smooth triangular prisms and the future's collision belts as round clumps. Both came from the source: Scotese drew the older belts as smooth envelopes, and the future's were smooth domes over the patches where two plates overlap, so neither had any of the ridge-and-valley relief a real range is made of, and the lighting drew each smooth envelope as two faces and a crest. Now every range is cut by branching valleys that run down its flanks, with massifs and passes along its crest, grown from the belt's own slope and only where the source left them out; and the future's collisions build long mountain chains with plateaus behind them instead of domes.

sections.name: Deep-time ranges
items: Transverse valleys, spurs, massifs and passes on every range the source drew smooth: the Central Pangean Mountains, the Caledonides, the Appalachian and Variscan belts, the Urals, the Gondwanan belts and the generated Precambrian ones. Tributaries branch off the valleys down to a kilometre across at the closest zoom.
The relief rides its crust through playback -- a valley stays where it is from one keyframe to the next instead of dissolving into another.
The snowline and the bare rock follow the ridges, valley floors are darker and crests lighter, and the shadowed side of a range shows its valleys instead of one dark face.

Measured, not assumed: inside mountain belts the fine relief is 84 m at 1 km and 176 m at 2.2 km of elevation today, and 16-44 m in the Palaeozoic. Only that shortfall is filled, so the present day and the Cenozoic keep their own valleys untouched.

sections.name: The future
items: Where continents collide in the next 250 million years the land now rises into long mountain chains along the collision, as wide as the collision is, with a plateau behind and uplands around -- not a smooth dome over the overlap.
Land above 1-3 km is where it was; what moved is the high ground: 2.5 million square kilometres above 4 km at +250 Myr (today 2.7, before 0.4), the highest summit 6.5 km.

sections.name: Behind it
items: A per-keyframe relief deficit (build/relief_deficit.py) says how much ridge-and-valley relief a real belt of that height carries that the source never drew; the shader grows exactly that with an erosion filter steered by the belt's slope.
Fingerprint whorls that circled the high ground of deep-time ranges at close zoom are gone: a texture term that bent its noise round every dome was retired.

The conditions readout shows how much of the world is under ice, and how much fainter or brighter the Sun was, again: both had quietly dropped out of the data at an earlier rebuild, so every glaciation read as ice-free.

releases.title: The curated seas at genus level, and the Cryogenian and Cambrian by block
releases.summary: The sixth flora-and-fauna pass, and the last of the handoff's queue. The curated record of the seas -- written before the registry had genera -- said 'Ammonoidea', 'Fusulinida', 'Graptolithina' on sixty-three spans; each is replaced by two or three genera of that group that lived there then, chosen by the same place rules every card obeys, with the curated prose kept on the first of them. Fifty-four new names fill the Cryogenian interglacials, the last Ediacaran tubes, the ten million years of small shelly fossils before the trilobites, and the Cambrian of each block from its first trilobite to the Furongian. Class-level names on the curated cards fell by more than half; the Precambrian's generic share from 42 to 38 per cent.

sections.name: In the seas
items: The curated oceans by name: the Ural Ocean's Devonian is Sporadoceras, Cymaclymenia and Manticoceras, its Permian Marginifera and Waagenoconcha; the Iapetus and Tornquist seas carry Didymograptus, Tetragraptus and Rhabdinopora; the Rheic Ocean's Carboniferous is Dombarites, Pericyclus and Goniatites; the Tethys of the Jurassic Perisphinctes and Dactylioceras, Ichthyosaurus and Ophthalmosaurus, Rhomaleosaurus, Plesiosaurus and Cryptoclidus; the Gulf of Mexico's rudist rim is Durania and Hippurites, its open water Placenticeras, Baculites and Pachydiscus; the Kaskaskia Sea's placoderms are Coccosteus, Groenlandaspis and Dunkleosteus; Pangaea's gorgonopsians Inostrancevia and Gorgonops.

The Cryogenian between the snowballs: Bavlinella and Leiosphaeridia, the Datangpo microfossils, the Twitya discs, the Fifteenmile scale microfossils. The last Ediacaran tubes: Vendotaenia, Sinotubulites, Corumbella, Gaojiashania, Conotubus. The first ten million years of the Cambrian: Protohertzina, Watsonella, Lapworthella, Sunnaginia, Tommotia, Hyolithellus, Coleoloides, Rhombocorniculum, Halkieria, the Shackleton Limestone reefs.

The first trilobite of each block -- Fallotaspis in Morocco and Nevada, Profallotaspis in Siberia, Callavia in Avalonia, Abadiella in Australia, Yunnanocephalus at Chengjiang -- then Kootenia, Olenoides, Ogygopsis and Bathyuriscus of Laurentia, Estaingia and Balcoracania of Emu Bay, Xystridura, the agnostoids Peronopsis, Pagetia, Glyptagnostus, Agnostotes and Lotagnostus that date the late Cambrian everywhere, Saukia, Dikelocephalus and Elvinia of Laurentia, Chuangia and Kaolishania of North China, Proceratopyge; the Alum Shale, Kaili, Wheeler Shale and Sirius Passet faunas.

sections.name: The right place
items: Avalonia's and the Mediterranean province's Ordovician trilobites -- Trinucleus, Selenopeltis, Placoparia, Colpocoryphe, Ectillaenus, Onnia, Neseuretus -- stay off Baltica, the mirror of last release's rule that kept Baltica's off Avalonia.
The warm-water larger foraminifera and rudists stop where the Tethyan platforms did: the Turgai Strait no longer offers Orbitolina.

sections.name: Keeping it right
items: taxa_src/upgrade_curated.py is the tool: it reads every curated span, finds the registry's genera of each class-level name that were alive and at home there, and replaces the name -- so the next batch of genera improves the curated cards too, by re-running it.
Measured by build/measure_generic.py: Cenozoic 20, Mesozoic 25, late Palaeozoic 25, early Palaeozoic 22, Precambrian 38 per cent; class-level curated slot-ages 6,188 to 2,840.

releases.title: Europe and eastern North America by crust, and the first seas at genus level
releases.summary: The fifth flora-and-fauna pass. Europe is two codes now -- Baltica and Avalonia in the north, the Gondwanan terranes that are France, Iberia, Bohemia and the Balkans in the south -- and eastern North America is two as well, the Laurentian craton and the Avalon and Carolina terranes that arrived with the Appalachians. So the Silurian myriapods of Scotland stay off Armorica, and the Mistaken Point fronds stay off Laurentia. Eighty-two genera fill the Tonian cratons, the Ediacaran assemblages and the Cambrian to Silurian shelves that were still 'Trilobita, Orthida, Dasycladales'. Class-level marine slots in the early Palaeozoic fell from 38 to 21 per cent.

sections.name: In the seas
items: The Tonian: the Atar Group microfossils of Mauritania and the Rasthof cap-carbonate mats of Namibia; Chuaria, Tawuia and the billion-year fungus Ourasphaira. The Ediacaran: Vendia, Cyclomedusa, Aspidella, Eoandromeda, Inaria, Palaeopascichnus, the Nama reef-builder Namapoikia, Nasepia, Shaanxilithes, the Mistaken Point fronds Beothukis, Trepassia and Pectinifrons, Haootia with its muscles, the Doushantuo acritarchs and embryos, the Miaohe seaweeds.

The Cambrian to Silurian by block: the Moroccan trilobites Hupetina and Cambropallas, the Bohemian Ellipsocephalus, Conocoryphe and Eccaparadoxides, the Tremadocian olenids Parabolina, Jujuyaspis and Kainella of Argentina and Oaxaca, the Mediterranean-province trilobites Selenopeltis, Placoparia, Colpocoryphe, Ectillaenus, Onnia and Dalmanitina, Baltica's Ogygiocaris and Trinucleus; the zone graptolites from Rhabdinopora to Saetograptus; the conodonts Cordylodus, Iapetognathus, Ozarkodina and Icriodus; Lichenaria, Catenipora and Syringopora; Prasopora and Hallopora; Orthis, Sowerbyella, Strophomena and Eospirifer; the calcareous algae Vermiporella, Cyclocrinites, Dimorphosiphon and Palaeoporella; the Silurian fishes Thelodus, Loganellia, Birkenia, Jamoytius, Andreolepis, Guiyu and Entelognathus.
Sponges begin with the Cryogenian biomarkers, not in the Tonian.

sections.name: The right crust
items: Sixty pre-Carboniferous European taxa are now on one half of Europe or the other, by where their collections are (Baltica's Asaphus and Megistaspis, the Rhynie chert, East Kirkton, Cowie Harbour; Bohemia's Reedops and Anarcestes, the Montagne Noire's Meganeura), and Baltica's own trilobites stay off Avalonia, which sat thirty degrees away until the Silurian.

The Avalon Peninsula, Nova Scotia, the Boston basin and the Carolina slate belt are one code, Gondwanan until the Silurian; the Mistaken Point fronds keep to the Avalon Peninsula, and Laurentia at 565 million years shows the rangeomorphs of the Mackenzie Mountains and nothing from Newfoundland.

sections.name: Keeping it right
items: The PBDB evidence attached to every entry is re-binned under the current region table by taxa_src/recode_regions.py, offline, so a code split is checked by the record the same day.

The refinement table had fifty-one names written in two rounds, and Python keeps only the last entry for a repeated key: Quercus lost its box when a later round gave it a range. The table now merges repeated names field by field.
Measured by build/measure_generic.py: marine slot-ages at class or order level, Cenozoic 22, Mesozoic 26, late Palaeozoic 27, early Palaeozoic 38 to 21, Precambrian 51 to 42 per cent.

releases.title: The late Palaeozoic seas, the ages between the samples, and Australia and China by block
releases.summary: The fourth flora-and-fauna pass. Forty-seven genera fill the Devonian, Carboniferous and Permian shelves outside North America and the Ediacaran sea floor. The placement listing was read at the fourteen ages between the ones already read, and about seventy placements fixed. Four region codes became eight: East Asia is now North China, South China, Indochina and Sibumasu, and Australia is east and west, so the Chengjiang fauna, the Cathaysian coal flora, the Glossopteris flora and the Winton dinosaurs each sit on their own block. The Tethyan Himalaya rides India, as its rock does.

sections.name: In the seas
items: The Devonian reef and shelf: Palmatolepis and Polygnathus conodonts, Schizophoria and Athyris, the trilobites Reedops and Gerastos, the goniatites Anarcestes, Sporadoceras and Cymaclymenia, the Canning Basin reef fauna, the Malvinokaffric Metacryphaeus. The Carboniferous: Siphonodella, the horn corals Siphonodendron and Caninia, Elonichthys, Eomarginifera, Dombarites, Fenestella, Spirifer, the cold-water Levipustula. The Permian: Spinomarginifera, Neochonetes, Orthothetina, Permophricodothyris, Paratirolites at the very end, Dielasma, Schizodus, the Gondwanan Terrakea, Echinalosia and Ingelarella, the last fusulinid seas' Spirigerella and Enteletes. The Ediacaran: Charniodiscus, Thectardis, Andiva, Parvancorina, Arkarua, Swartpuntia.
The Lago Mare card is a brackish lake: killifish, charophytes, dreissenid mussels and tamarisk, and the mastodons and dawn redwoods stay on the land cards around it.

sections.name: The right place, fourth pass
items: Read at 5, 15, 40, 60, 90, 110, 170, 190, 215, 265, 320, 375, 420 and 480 million years ago. Hipparion, the chalicotheres and Mammut no longer stand at 71 N in a Pliocene that was forest, and the tundra labels begin at 2.8 million years with the ice; the anthracotheres leave Europe when they did; brontotheres, entelodonts and Andrewsarchus keep to the continents and basins that hold them; carcharodontosaurs, brachiosaurs and spinosaurs to their own decades of the Cretaceous; Plateosaurus, Eudimorphodon and Metoposaurus to the Germanic basin, Coelophysis and Placerias to the Chinle; the Triassic dicynodonts and rauisuchians to the crust that has their bones; gorgonopsians to the Karoo and the Russian platform; Baragwanathia to Victoria, and the Silurian myriapods of Scotland off the Gondwanan terranes that are France today.

The swimming sloth Thalassocnus stays on the Pisco coast. The Cathaysian flora stops at the Solonker suture, so Amuria is Angaran on both its province and its list. The Tethyan Himalaya was riding the Lhasa terrane at 12 N while India was at 43 S; it sits on India now, and a third detector holds every label's plate against its home crust so the next one cannot.

sections.name: Keeping it right
items: Region codes: as-ne, as-s, as-ic, as-sb replace the two East Asian codes and au-w, au-e the Australian one; the old codes survive as aliases, so nothing written before this release changed meaning. Labels named differently from the province model's blocks (Amuria, Annamia, Greater Adria, the Lhasa terrane and eleven more) keep their own block instead of the nearest one.

The measure of how generic the marine cards still are is a script now (build/measure_generic.py), run on two releases side by side: at class and order level, Cenozoic 22, Mesozoic 26, late Palaeozoic 28 to 27, early Palaeozoic 38, Precambrian 51 per cent of marine slot-ages. The numbers quoted before this release used a counting nobody wrote down and are not comparable.

releases.title: The Triassic and Cretaceous seas, the polar oceans, and every age read
releases.summary: The third flora-and-fauna pass. Every card at the eleven ages not yet read -- from the late Miocene to the Ediacaran -- was listed organism by organism and read, and about fifty placements fixed. Sixty-two genera fill the seas that were still thin: the Triassic shelves, the Early Cretaceous, the Southern Ocean, the Arctic and the Paratethys. The class-level curated lists of Ordovician Laurentia, Baltica and Siberia are rewritten with the genera the record actually names.

sections.name: In the seas
items: The Triassic at genus level: Eumorphotis and Unionites in the seas after the great dying, Flexoptychites and Gymnotoceras, the crinoid gardens of the Muschelkalk, nothosaurs, Henodus, Psiloceras at the base of the Jurassic. The Early Cretaceous: Neocomites, Olcostephanus, Crioceratites, Deshayesites, Douvilleiceras, the Boreal Polyptychites, the giant Tropaeum and Umoonasaurus of the Eromanga sea, Orbitolina of the Urgonian reefs.

The polar oceans: krill, silverfish and toothfish, crabeater and harp seals, orcas and humpbacks, sea butterflies and sea angels, geoducks, cold-water scallops and bryozoan thickets; the Arctic Ocean's card now names its bowhead, narwhal, polar cod, walrus and sea-ice algae. The Paratethys gets its Sarmatian cockles and horn snails.
Class-level entries on marine cards: early Palaeozoic 45 to 36 per cent, Mesozoic 51 to 40, Cenozoic 37 to 33.

sections.name: The right place, third pass
items: Read at 10, 35, 80, 120, 200, 230, 280, 350, 450, 500 and 600 million years ago. Sivapithecus stays in the Siwaliks and Anatolia; the Amazon's giant caimans and turtles stay in Amazonia; Australopithecus-age apes stay where their fossils are; ceratopsids reach Asia only for the two million years Sinoceratops did; hadrosaurs reach the south only at the very end; Archaeopteryx's neighbour Scelidosaurus stays in Dorset; Jehol's animals stay in Liaoning; the Angaran and Cathaysian floras stop at their own provinces; the warm Laurentian shelf fauna no longer reaches the cold Gondwanan margin; South China's biotas stay off North China's card.
Wrangellia, an oceanic plateau, and Wallacea before its islands rose are sea cards. The Caledonides shed the Appalachians' animals once the Atlantic opened.

sections.name: Kept honest
items: The early Palaeozoic continents' own lists name Cameroceras, Flexicalymene, Rafinesquina, Asaphus, Heliolites and Atrypa where they named 'Brachiopoda' and 'Crinoidea'.
Every new organism was cross-examined against the Paleobiology Database, and the batch sources carry the verdicts.

releases.title: Deeper seas, older land, and six labels put back on their own continent
releases.summary: A second pass over the flora and fauna. The catalogue grows from about 1,150 organisms to 1,320, most of them the animals and plants of the Palaeozoic and Mesozoic seas and of Devonian to Permian land outside Europe and North America, so a Silurian sea or a Permian Siberia now names its trilobites, sharks and seed ferns instead of its phyla. Every card at eight sample ages from the Pliocene to the Devonian was read by eye and the placements the rules could not see were fixed. Six labels that had been drawn on the wrong continent -- the Gilboa Forest of New York was riding Brazil to the South Pole -- now sit where they belong.

sections.name: In the seas
items: Ninety-one genera from the Cambrian to the Cretaceous: Marrella and Opabinia in the Sauk Sea, Flexicalymene and Orthoceras in the Ordovician, Calymene and Eurypterus in the Silurian, Phacops and Cladoselache in the Devonian, Archimedes and Pentremites in the Carboniferous, Leedsichthys and Metriorhynchus in the Jurassic, Elasmosaurus and Pteranodon over the Western Interior Seaway. Where a card can name four animals by genus, the class-level names stand down to one.
The sea's own plants: dasyclad and coralline algae, Solenopora, Girvanella and the phylloid algae that built Permian reefs, where every sea had shown only 'green algae, red algae'.
Class-level entries on marine cards fell from 82 to 45 per cent in the early Palaeozoic, 79 to 44 in the late, and 63 to 51 in the Mesozoic.

sections.name: On the land before the dinosaurs
items: Devonian to Permian life beyond Europe and North America: the Aztec fishes of Antarctica, the Xinhang forest of China, Bradysaurus, Diictodon and Procynosuchus in the Karoo, Deltavjatia and Suminia at Kotelnich, the Kuznetsk coal forests of Siberia, and the Cathaysian seed ferns of Permian China.

Glaciated Gondwana, 335 to 290 million years ago, is now polar ground: its cards show the springtails, mites, mosses, Nothorhacopteris and Botrychiopsis of the country between the ice sheets, where before the polar rule did not reach that far back.

The Tonian and Cryogenian, block by block: the Bitter Springs, Chuar, Svanbergfjellet, Lakhanda and Liulaobei assemblages, the first green seaweeds (Proterocladus, Longfengshania) and the named acritarchs of the world before the snowball. Seventeen Precambrian labels had shared one identical list.

sections.name: The right place, again
items: Every card at 3, 20, 50, 100, 150, 250, 300 and 400 million years ago was listed organism by organism and read: Australopithecus off the Atlas, edelweiss off the Urals, Archaeopteryx confined to Solnhofen, Allosaurus and Stegosaurus to Portugal and the Morrison, Lystrosaurus off Scotland, Rufloria out of China, Psaronius out of Patagonia, and about sixty more.

Six labels authored at their ancient positions had been tracked on whatever continent lies there today: the Gilboa Forest, the Acadian Belt, the Oslo Rift, the Rotliegend Desert, the Zechstein Sea and the Solnhofen Lagoon now ride their own crust, and a check derived from each label's home crust will catch the next one.

Curated lists that overlapped in time were silently losing taxa: Basilosaurus never reached Africa's Eocene card. They are merged now. Life that fell into a sea -- Archaeopteryx into the Solnhofen lagoon -- and seas that lay over a continent -- the Muschelkalk's nothosaurs on Eurasia's Triassic card -- appear under their own headings.
The Arctic Azolla Bloom is a sea card with the fern on it. Kerguelen's Cretaceous conifer forest, known from wood in drill cores, has its own list and says that no land animal is known from it.

sections.name: Drawings
items: Seventeen body plans that no silhouette library holds -- belemnite, conodont, blastoid, bryozoan, horn coral, rudist, stromatoporoid, zosterophyll, progymnosperm, astrapothere, embrithopod, mesosaur, ostracod, uncoiled ammonite, bamboo, Namacalathus and agnostid -- are drawn by hand. No organism on any card is drawn as its parent group any more; the count was 33 in release 3.5.

Five files the app asked for on every load did not exist. The future keyframes now carry their foreland basins, the one field that truly does not exist is declared, and the build refuses to publish a page that fetches a file the site lacks.

releases.title: Flora and fauna, rebuilt: the right life, in the right place, with the right picture
releases.summary: Every card's list of organisms now comes from one catalogue of about 1,150 plants, animals and microbes, each recorded with when it lived, where it lived and what it looked like. A card shows only what was alive at that moment on that ground, always with animals and plants side by side, and every one of the 38,000 card-and-age combinations the app can show is checked before release. The errors this replaces were real ones: bison in North America sixty million years early, moose in Patagonia, a bear drawn as a coyote, ants and crocodiles on a plateau two kilometres under the Pacific.

sections.name: The right picture
items: An organism's drawing now follows from what it is, not from its name. Bears are drawn as bears, ground sloths as ground sloths, the hoofed mammals of South America as hoofed mammals, and kelp as kelp — where before a fallback quietly drew any unmatched land animal as a small reptile and any sea creature as a fish.

About 350 more organisms have their own traced silhouette, from the dodo and the sperm whale to the vampire squid. Where no honest drawing exists for a body plan, the card uses the nearest relative's outline and the build keeps count: 30 such cases, down from 33, and the number is only allowed to fall.

sections.name: The right time and place
items: Each card is filtered by age and by the crust it sits on. North America at 60 million years ago shows multituberculates, early hoofed mammals and dawn redwood, not bison; Patagonia shows guanaco and rhea, not moose and wolverine.

Narrow endemics stay where they live. Giant sequoia is on the Sierra Nevada and not the Gulf of California; Amazon river dolphins are in Amazonia and not Lake Titicaca; edelweiss is on the Alps and not the Urals; alligators are out of the Great Lakes.
Every land card after the first forests shows both fauna and flora, under their own headings. None shows fewer than four organisms unless the card says why.

sections.name: Seas, ocean islands and the poles
items: Features that lie under water are now sea cards. The Shatsky Rise, Ontong Java, the Walvis Ridge and the other drowned plateaus show sperm whales, giant squid, lanternfish and cold-water corals. The Gulf of California and the Red Sea become seas at the dates the water actually came in, about 7 and 20 million years ago.

Mid-ocean ridges show vent life and the open ocean above it, without the seaweeds and coastal clams that had crept on to them. The tropical Atlantic and the eastern Pacific have their own headings; every warm sea used to be labelled Indo-Pacific.

Ocean islands show what reached them. Kerguelen has king penguins, elephant seals and Kerguelen cabbage, and — in the Miocene — the conifer forest whose wood lies between its lava flows. Mauritius has the dodo and giant tortoises until the present day, then what survived them. The Seychelles have their ancient frogs, the coco de mer and giant tortoises. Jan Mayen has little auks, fulmars and dwarf willow.

Antarctica after the ice came shows only what is known from it: mosses, lichens, springtails, the tundra weevils of the Transantarctic Mountains, penguins and seals. High-Arctic ground shows muskox, Arctic hare and mountain avens instead of beaver and lodgepole pine. Lake Vostok shows microbes, and says why that is all.

sections.name: Kept honest
items: The catalogue was cross-checked against the Paleobiology Database for classification, age range and where fossils have been found; every disagreement was either corrected or recorded with its reason.

A release is now refused if any card shows an organism outside its lifetime, off its crust, outside its own range within a region, under a drawing of something else, or lists land life on ground the globe draws as deep sea.

releases.title: One ambient view, with its own small controls
releases.summary: The Ambient button now opens the ambient globe itself over the window — the turning Earth with time running and the clouds — in place of the old in-app mode that only hid the controls. It starts at the age you were looking at, and coming back hands that age (and whether time was running) back to the main view.

sections.name: Ambient
items: Top left: Close, back to the main view (Escape does the same), and Full screen.

Top right: Pause/Play, which stops time only — the globe keeps turning and the weather keeps moving — and the geological eras: Neoproterozoic, Paleozoic, Mesozoic, Cenozoic and the projected Future, each a jump to the start of that era, whether time is running or paused; the era you are in is lit.
The old in-app ambient mode is gone. The page still runs on its own as a screensaver or wallpaper, and ?ui=0 hides its controls and readout there.

releases.title: The Ambient page gets the clouds, and the update log is whole again
releases.summary: The background build — the slowly turning Earth that runs as a screensaver or wallpaper — now carries the same NASA cloud deck as the app, moving on its own clock and arranged by each era's coasts, vegetation and ice, and its frames no longer hitch at every keyframe. This log also regains eight releases from August that were written but never reached the site.

sections.name: Ambient
items: Clouds over the ambient globe: NASA's Blue Marble cloud field in the same slow coherent motion as the app's, thickening, merging and dissolving on its own clock, thinner over dry land and a frozen world, lit by the same terminator. Their arrangement follows the colours of the world sheets (water, green land, dry land, ice), since this page carries no climate fields; there is no cloud shadow. ?clouds=0 turns them off, ?weather=0 holds them still, and reduced-motion settings hold them still too.
No more hitch at a keyframe crossing: each world sheet and the cloud image reach the graphics card in strips across frames instead of in one piece at the moment they are first drawn.

Time and rotation now advance by the time since the previous drawn frame. The 30 fps cap had been counting the previous tick instead, so time ran at half the requested speed and both motions stuttered whenever the tick pattern broke.

sections.name: Update log
items: Eight releases from 5–9 August 2026 (2.3 to 3.0: the monsoon, the deserts, Siberia's forests and more) had been written into the build's log but never copied to the site. They are here now, and the three September releases that had reused their numbers are 3.1 to 3.3.

releases.title: Clouds that live through playback, and continents that drift instead of jumping
releases.summary: The same day's second round, from the owner's own screenshots. The clouds now stay on while time runs and evolve on their own clock: masses thicken, merge across a clearing and dissolve, arranged by where each era's land, rain, ice and the zonal circulation make cloud likely, with the satellite structure kept inside them. And the wide view no longer looks like an unfinished frame: the app draws from 4096-wide world sheets on a desktop, takes them earlier when the graphics chip is struggling, and time now waits for a keyframe's fields before moving on, so a continent in motion drifts rather than snapping.

sections.name: Clouds
items: Cloud cover persists through Play. The deck's transport runs on its own weather clock while the timeline runs, and its arrangement follows the continents, the era's modelled rainfall, its ice and a soft zonal climatology: the tropical convergence band, the mid-latitude storm tracks and the clear subtropical belts.

Clouds evolve. A slow synoptic gate (about a minute from clear to overcast at any one place, and moved gently by the era as well) thickens, merges and dissolves cloud masses; the fine fronts and spirals inside them are still the satellite field in coherent motion. A snowball world loses most of its deck.

The clouds never see a half-arrived world: playback waits for the next keyframe's fields before it advances, and the deck fades only for the schematic shading, your own switch, or a preview standing in.

sections.name: Timeline
items: The wide view draws from 4096-wide world sheets on a desktop, twice the previous resolution; the 2048 set stays for the Ambient page and for devices with little memory. Once the quality governor has stepped the render scale down, the sheets take over earlier, since a pre-shaded sheet is sharper than the live shader at half resolution and a tenth of its cost.

A jump now switches from the coarse preview to the full terrain only when the keyframe's elevation, rainfall, lakes, surface processes, ocean structure, motion and plate coordinates are all here, instead of on elevation alone, which had put a new coastline over the previous age's lakes and drainage for a second.

Playback waits for a keyframe's fields the way it already waited for a late sheet (never more than a second and a half), so continents drift through a crossing instead of snapping to a still and back.

No single frame moves time by more than 1.5 million years, whatever the speed: fast playback on a slow frame now runs a little below the slider, smoothly, where it used to leap half an interval at once.

The hitch at every keyframe crossing is gone: the small elevation map the place-names snap to was being read back from the full-size keyframe on the spot, once per keyframe; it is now prepared in the background.

releases.title: Real clouds in motion, a seek that answers at once, and a temperature curve
releases.summary: Three things brought over from the Tectonic Atlas experiment, on top of the original globe rather than in place of it: NASA's Blue Marble cloud field drifting over the paused globe and map, a timeline that shows the age you asked for the moment you ask (a coarse preview first, the full terrain a fraction of a second later, instead of the old world sitting there under the new age for several seconds), and a graph of the modelled global mean temperature across the whole 1.25 billion years under the conditions readout. The terrain, the ocean floor, the mountains, the controls and the science are exactly as before: the cloud-off picture matches the previous release to within the harness's own noise.

sections.name: Clouds
items: The clouds are now NASA's Blue Marble cloud composite (NASA/Goddard Space Flight Center, image by Reto Stöckli), one continuous field in slow coherent motion, so fronts stay connected and storms stay single instead of dissolving into noise cells. The image loads only after the terrain is ready and costs nothing until then.

Each era adapts the field: its own land and modelled rainfall set where the deck thins and thickens, so Pangaea's dry interior clears while its monsoon coasts stay cloudy. Ancient and future ages show satellite-derived structure with illustrative climate adaptation, not the weather of any real day.

Clouds and their shadows leave the moment you press Play and return when you pause, so playback shows the surface. Cloud cover and Animate weather are separate switches under Atmosphere; the animation starts off if your system asks for reduced motion.
The clouds now thin as you come close rather than vanishing, and they cover the flat map as well as the globe, with one shared clock.

sections.name: Timeline
items: A jump to an age whose terrain is not loaded yet shows that age at once, coarsely, from a preview of all 251 keyframes, and the readout says Loading terrain until the full-detail fields arrive; measured from a warm server, full detail follows in a quarter to half a second where it used to take three to nine seconds with the previous age left on screen.

Requests follow you: a run of jumps cancels the downloads for ages you left behind instead of draining them ahead of the one you stopped on, and the neighbourhood kept warm now follows the playback speed and the measured connection instead of warming the whole timeline.
Pressing a marker or stepping onto an exact keyframe now binds that keyframe alone; it used to bind its neighbour's interval fields (the present day read the +5 Myr keyframe's plate motion).
A press anywhere on the era names or the scale seeks there and drags like the slider, and the slider itself is easier to grab.
A lost packet no longer makes a field disappear until reload: only a real 404 marks a field absent, and everything else is retried.

sections.name: Conditions
items: The conditions readout carries a graph of the modelled global mean temperature across the whole timeline, 1,000 Ma at the left and +250 Myr at the right, with the selected age marked and its value shown. It is the same modelled curve the Avg temp line prints, drawn straight through the 251 records, and the same caveats apply.

sections.name: Performance
items: With the clouds moving over a paused globe, the ground is rendered once and kept, refreshed a strip at a time so the sea sheen keeps moving, and only the cloud layer is redrawn each weather frame; the terrain itself is drawn at full resolution as before and the cloud-off frame is unchanged.
The quality governor no longer reads weather frames as a slow machine: it judges playback and interaction only.

releases.title: The wide view draws from baked sheets, and the clock slows down
releases.summary: Zoomed out, the globe now draws from a pre-rendered sheet of each keyframe instead of running the full terrain shader on every pixel, which is what makes playback smooth on modest hardware and lets the Ambient page run all day. Underneath, a first round of the mountain and plains models landed, with its fold ridges deliberately held back until they look like ranges.

sections.name: Performance
items: The wide view and the Ambient page draw from 251 baked world sheets. Time waits briefly for a sheet rather than falling back to the heavy shader, and playback looks a few keyframes ahead so it rarely has to wait.
Playback runs at 3 Myr per second by default and 10 at most. 18 was crossing a keyframe every quarter second, faster than a landscape can be read or a sheet fetched.
A keyframe crossing no longer stalls the frame: every field is decoded and uploaded ahead of time, and the build refuses to ship if a crossing pays for uploads again.

sections.name: Landscape
items: Plains carry a faint valley texture that runs with the regional slope, from a drainage field baked from the reconstruction. The great sand seas carry dune lineation along the trade-wind line.
The foreland moat in front of a mountain belt no longer drowns dry plains.
Fold-belt ridges were built, reviewed on screen, and withheld: they read as ribbing rather than ranges. The model ships dormant behind a switch for the next round.

releases.title: Boreal forest, without flooding Pangaea
releases.summary: An earlier attempt at wetting the world's cold forested interiors worked for Siberia and quietly turned Permian Pangaea from a desert continent into a green one -- it was reverted. This is the same repair done with the distinction the first one lacked: water returned by a landscape depends on how cold it is, because cold ground loses far less of it, AND on whether anything is growing there to return it in the first place. Cold and vegetated gets the full effect; cold and bare -- the Gobi, the Great Basin -- gets almost none. Siberia greens toward the boreal forest it is, and the low-latitude heart of Pangaea stays the desert it was.

releases.title: Siberia stops being a desert
releases.summary: Central Siberia was modelled as dry as the Sahara -- the same number for 400 millimetres of rain a year as for fifteen. Water that falls on land evaporates and falls again further inland, and the model let that recycling fade over a fixed distance regardless of climate. But cold air holds what it carries far longer than hot air does, which is why boreal forest stretches thousands of kilometres from any ocean while a hot continental interior at the same distance is sand. Letting the recycling reach further where it is cold lifts the whole cold interior -- Siberia, the Canadian north, central Europe -- and leaves every desert exactly where it was.

releases.title: Deserts that look like sand
releases.summary: Measured against a true-colour photograph of the Earth, our biomes sat too close together in colour: the deserts not warm enough, the forests not deep enough, everything drifting toward the same middling tan. Widening the palette itself -- rather than turning a single saturation knob, which pulls both ends the same way and was tried and undone -- moves the Sahara, the Congo and the North American plains substantially closer to what a satellite sees. The Sahara in particular now reads as sand rather than pale khaki. One region moves the wrong way, and it is honest about why: Siberia comes out as cold DRY ground rather than the boreal forest it is, which is the rainfall model's problem and not the palette's.

releases.title: Arabia learns to be a desert
releases.summary: A monsoon does not just draw air in; it also pushes air down somewhere else, and that sinking is what keeps the great subtropical deserts dry. The model worked out where the sinking should fall, but it decided where the monsoons themselves were purely from latitude and the presence of land -- so the Deccan, which is drenched every summer, and the Rub al Khali, the driest sand on Earth, came out identical. Both sit at the same latitude and both are land. Deciding instead by where rain is actually falling makes India a strong source that dries Arabia downstream, while Arabia, having no storms of its own, pushes almost nothing back. Arabia and inland Australia now read as the deserts they are, and the deep-time supercontinents lose more of their banded look.

releases.title: A shallow sea is not an ocean
releases.summary: Air passing over water picked up as much moisture from the Black Sea or the Caspian as it would from the open Atlantic, which is not how evaporation works: a small enclosed sea has only so much water surface to give. The effect was easy to miss at present day -- it made the steppes north of the Black Sea come out wetter than the Congo -- and much larger in deep time, where shallow seas spread across the middle of the continents and every one of them was quietly watering the land around it. Weighting the supply by how much open water is actually upwind dries Pangaea's interior the way a supercontinent should be dry, and eases the banded look further, while the rainforests, which draw on real oceans, do not move at all.

releases.title: The monsoon finally arrives
releases.summary: Every high mountain range in the model was a desert. Air was allowed to travel east and west freely, but the only path that carries moisture from the ocean towards a pole was open solely in the mid-latitudes -- so the monsoon, which is that same movement happening much nearer the equator, had nowhere to go. The Himalayan front, one of the wettest places on Earth, was modelled as dry as the Sahara. Opening that path where monsoons actually occur, and stopping air from losing more water than it is carrying when it climbs, changes a great deal downstream: rainforests reach their real extent, the Congo and the Amazon finally stand in the right proportion to one another, rivers grow where mountains make them, and the banded look across the deep-time supercontinents eases further. The deserts are untouched -- the Sahara, the Gobi and the Atacama are as dry as they were.

releases.title: Mountains get their ridges into the light
releases.summary: A real mountain belt is dozens of parallel ridges, and ours kept rendering as a smooth swell with the ridges painted on as shading. The reason turned out to be arithmetic: the surface is lit by comparing heights about 23 km apart, and that comparison is exactly blind to detail spaced around 47 km -- which is the scale ridges and valleys actually occupy. No amount of putting the ridges into the height data could light them; a test at the largest realistic size moved the Himalaya by well under one part in a hundred. So the ridges now go straight into the surface's orientation instead, steered along each belt's own fold direction. They catch light and cast shade like the terrain they are, and the difference shows most when you are looking at a whole range.

releases.title: River corridors stop drawing the rain belts
releases.summary: Vegetation across the deep-time supercontinents was breaking into hard-edged green bands. The rainfall behind them turned out to be fine -- the fault was downstream, in the river corridors painted on top of it. Those corridors follow drainage, drainage follows rainfall, so every corridor traced the rain belt that fed it and the two signals stacked into a stripe. They were also simply too wide: a valley floor and its riparian edge were being drawn across country that a real river greens only in a thin ribbon. Narrowing them to something a river can actually water cuts the banding at 280 Ma by a third, and leaves the present day where it was -- the Congo, the Amazon and the North American plains are unchanged to the eye.

releases.title: Mountain ranges start to comb
releases.summary: A mountain belt is dozens of parallel ridges running along its length, and ours rendered as smooth swells. The machinery to draw that has existed for a long time and had never once run: it steers off a fold-direction field that was silently switching off at the present day, so it was being pointed by a direction of zero.

sections.name: Mountains
items: Ranges now show ridges running along strike rather than a single smooth swell. The Andes, the Zagros and the Alps get this for the first time — the plate reconstruction cannot see shortening inside an overriding plate, so the fabric now also reads a range's strike from the tangent to its own contours.

The fold fabric was switching off at the present day. The two keyframes either side of today are used together, and one of them was among only two in the whole series that shipped without a tectonic field — which silenced the feature for every age it touched. Both files are now built, and a missing one can no longer switch the system off.

releases.title: The sea floor around a volcano is not smooth
releases.summary: Around big volcanic rises like the Hawaiian chain, the ocean floor rendered as a large blank of smooth blue. The abyssal-hill texture is deliberately switched off over a volcano so it does not get combed across the edifice — but nothing was drawn in its place. It now gets the hummocky landslide-debris terrain such flanks really have.

sections.name: The ocean floor
items: Volcanic aprons have their own texture. The floor around a seamount or an island chain is buried in giant landslide debris — the fields off Hawaii contain blocks kilometres across — and it now reads that way instead of as a smooth halo hundreds of kilometres wide.
The new terrain is keyed to exactly the region the abyssal fabric gives up, so the two hand over to each other with no gap between them.
Detail measured on the frame rose by about half around the Scotia arc and by a sixth around Hawaii, with the land untouched.

releases.title: Rain that reaches the far side of a continent
releases.summary: The climate model had a fault that quietly mis-coloured every continent: it moved moisture only east and west, so the eastern United States came out drier than the Sahara. Fixing it turned the eastern seaboard green, gave the Amazon and the Congo the solid dark canopy they should have, and left the real deserts dry. Mountains now carry a proper treeline, deserts have sand seas and rock massifs instead of one flat tan, and the Great Lakes are back.

sections.name: Climate and vegetation
items: Moisture now travels north and south as well as east and west. Without that, the Atlantic and the Gulf sat downwind of nothing and eastern North America was fed by air that had already crossed the continent — it rendered drier than the Sahara. It now reads as forest, with the plains gold and the western interior brown, and the dry line where it belongs near the hundredth meridian.

Monsoon deserts sit in the right places. The model was casting the Indian monsoon's dry shadow eastward onto southeast Asia instead of westward onto Arabia, so the two were effectively swapped: the Rub al Khali rendered wetter than the Congo. Arabia is now sand and monsoon China is now forest.

Wet interiors keep their own water. The Amazon and the Congo were being dried for being far inland, when in fact a rainforest waters its own far side by evaporating what already fell on it. The Amazon had been drying westward — driest under the Andes, which is exactly backwards — and now holds its canopy across the basin.
Central Siberia reads as taiga rather than steppe, and the Sahel, the Chaco and the Kazakh steppe stayed where they were.

sections.name: Mountains
items: A treeline is a temperature, not an altitude. Bare rock used to begin at the same height everywhere on Earth — 1,700 m, which is alpine desert in Lapland and cloud forest in Ecuador. It now follows the climate, so ranges carry snow, then bare rock, then conifer, in bands that follow the ridge.
Dry ranges go bare much lower, because a treeline needs water as well as warmth. The arid Andes and the Tibetan Plateau read as rock and salt rather than scrub.

Bare rock takes light harder than forest does — no canopy to scatter it between the faces — so ridges stand out. The rock keeps the colour of the geology underneath it, so ranges are not all cut from the same grey stone.

sections.name: Deserts
items: A desert is not one tan. Sand seas the size of countries, orange dune fields, and dark rocky massifs now separate out, sorted by where sand can actually collect — flat ground with nothing to carry it away. The Grand Erg reads as a smooth sheet and the Hoggar stands out of it.

sections.name: Fixes
items: The Great Lakes are back, along with Baikal, Victoria, Titicaca and around eleven hundred other real lakes. A field rebuild had been overwriting their true outlines with the water-balance solver's own guess.
The bright magenta spots that appeared in valleys and rift lakes are gone.
Labels no longer disappear when zoomed out, no feature is labelled twice, and the Tethys, Palaeo-Tethys and Neotethys no longer all point at the same water.

Every feature card has been read for typographical errors, and sixty-seven of them checked against the published literature — several described a mountain range as though its peaks were as old as its rocks, which is usually wrong by hundreds of millions of years.
The camera moves in proportion to how far you are zoomed in, so close views are steerable.
The Schematic view has been retired; Satellite is now the only view, and the Geological Intervals panel starts closed.

releases.title: Tilt the Earth, and a globe that fits your phone
releases.summary: You can now lean the camera over and look at the horizon, with real three-dimensional terrain under it. The sea floor is smooth again — the stair-step pattern is gone, and this time for the right reason. Land cards list the animals that lived there, not only the plants.

sections.name: The ocean floor
items: The staircase is gone. Zoomed in, the deep ocean was crossed by large angular slabs — flat panels of constant shade with long straight edges and square corners, tens of degrees across, at every age.

The cause was in the crust's age, not in the picture. Where there is no survey data the model works out how old each patch of sea floor is by finding the nearest dated stripe and copying its age wholesale — done separately for each plate. That builds a mosaic of flat tiles with a hard step at every edge, and the plate edges are long and straight. At 615 million years ago the jump between two neighbouring cells was 70 million years of age, which the depth-versus-age law turns into a wall 1,349 m high across 25 km. A real abyssal plain changes by 50 to 125 m.

Crustal age now varies smoothly away from a spreading ridge, which is what it does in nature. Measured across the whole timeline the step is now 55 to 72 m at every age, inside the physical range. Surveyed sea floor is untouched and still wins exactly where it exists.

Three quarters of the ocean's "fracture zone" scars turned out to be this artefact and have gone with it. Before the Cambrian, where there has never been any survey data, 92 per cent of them were invented by the model's own tile edges. Real scars survive to within a rounding error.
Earlier attempts fixed two other real defects that were not this one — the image format's four-pixel compression blocks, and the way the shelf edge was detected — and both improvements are kept.

sections.name: The future
items: Mountains now wear down. The future was built by rotating today's terrain into new positions, and nothing in it could erode: every present-day range was still standing at its present height a quarter of a billion years from now. Land above 2 km and above 3 km were identical to today's, to the decimal.

Relief now decays with time, fast for peaks and valleys and slowly for high plateaus, calibrated so that a range like the Appalachians — above 4 km when Pangaea assembled, 1 to 2 km today — wears down at the right rate.

New mountains rise where continents actually collide. Where two landmasses' paths overlap, that overlap is the convergence, and it used to be calculated and then thrown away — 12.8 million square kilometres of it, larger than the whole Alpine–Himalayan belt. It now drives crustal thickening, so a collision builds a range instead of two outlines passing through each other.
Rifted coasts subside and gain a shelf, so a continent that splits off no longer keeps its original knife-edge outline for 250 million years.

The future's own staircase is gone too. Its coastlines were quantised to half a degree — six times coarser than the map they were drawn on — and its elevations were sampled without smoothing. Both now work at the map's own resolution, and the coastline is a quarter less jagged by measurement.

sections.name: Life on land
items: Land cards now show animals. Every land region in the model was described by a vegetation scheme and nothing else, so a card for a continent said what grew there and never what lived there — flowers and forests, no animals, across the whole timeline.

All eighteen land provinces now list their fauna alongside their flora: the first air-breathing millipede in the Silurian, giant dragonflies and 2.5 m millipedes in the coal forests, Lystrosaurus after the end-Permian, Archaeopteryx in the Jurassic, mammoths and muskoxen on the tundra. Forty-eight animals were added, each with its own description.
A check now fails the build if any land region lists plants and no animals, so this cannot quietly come back.

sections.name: One frame in particular
items: The Mediterranean at 5 million years ago is drawn as the salt desert it was. Between 5.97 and 5.33 million years ago the Gibraltar gateway closed and the sea evaporated faster than its rivers could refill it, leaving a desert floored by up to 2 km of salt, with brine lakes in the deepest basins and the Nile cutting a canyon kilometres deep to reach the new base level. It ended in a flood that refilled the entire basin in perhaps a few months.

Two honest compromises, both worth stating: keyframes step 5 million years, so a 640,000-year event is drawn on the nearest one; and the app draws sea wherever the ground is below sea level, so a surface that was both dry and 1.5 km below the Atlantic cannot be expressed exactly — the salt flats are lifted just enough to read as exposed ground.

sections.name: Looking around
items: Tilt and Heading sliders, with Reset to north, sit under the timeline. Tilt leans the camera off vertical the way Google Earth does, so you can look across the landscape to a curved horizon instead of only straight down at a disc.

The terrain is genuinely three-dimensional now. It used to be a perfectly smooth ball with the relief painted on by shading — which is convincing looking straight down and falls apart the moment you tilt, because a shaded sphere seen edge-on is still a sphere. The elevation now shapes the surface itself, so mountains stand against the sky and the sea floor has real depth. Height is exaggerated when you come in close, and not at all when you are far out, where you could not see it anyway.
Dragging works the same at any heading. Left and right always move the globe left and right on screen, even after you have turned the compass — the drag is rotated to match where you are facing.
A spin-speed slider next to the time speed, for when auto-rotate is on.
In map view, arrows pan east and west so you can look at any face of the Earth rather than one fixed half. Labels, plate boundaries and click targets all pan with it.

sections.name: On a phone
items: The globe now owns the screen. The conditions panel had no mobile layout at all and rendered at full desktop width straight over the map, and the left-hand timeline was hidden outright rather than made reachable. Both are now drawers behind their own button, one open at a time, and touching the globe closes them.

Landscape is handled too. A phone turned sideways is wider than the threshold that decides 'this is a small screen' and less than half as tall, so it had been getting the full desktop layout squeezed into 360 pixels of height. Height is now what decides it, and the controls collapse to a single row.

Pinch to zoom works on the globe instead of the page. Two fingers used to scale the whole browser window, because the app only ever listened for one finger and the gesture was the browser's before any of our code saw it. The canvas now claims touch gestures for itself and tracks both fingers, so the zoom follows the distance between them.
An Era labels button sits on the right, so the one layer worth turning on and off — the thing that tells you what you are looking at — no longer needs a panel opened to reach it.

releases.title: Rain that knows where the sea is
releases.summary: A second pass over the research programme. The weather now responds to the shallow seas the last release added, the deep ocean floor has depth again, and eleven places were found riding the wrong continent.

sections.name: Climate and weather
items: Rainfall now knows about the shelf seas. The wind-and-moisture model was still running on a map without them, so flooding the Triassic changed the coastline without making the air over it any wetter. Land that stayed land is 17% wetter at 240 Ma, and the deep Pangaean interior 11%.

The climate readout names the state from the temperature it is showing you. It used to use a separate internal measure, so at 250 Ma the panel read “28.5 °C” and “Hothouse” side by side — while 28.5 °C is a warm greenhouse on the scale being quoted.

No grasslands before there were grasses. The world at 100 million years ago was being drawn with grassy plains and savanna stipple; grasses only matter ecologically from about 40 Ma, and tropical savanna from about 8 Ma.

sections.name: The ocean floor
items: A third of the sea floor was perfectly flat. Everything older than about 97 million years was drawn at exactly the same depth — 6,000 m — across the whole old Pacific and the old North Atlantic. Real sea floor keeps deepening, more slowly, and now so does this one.
Old crust sits about 400 m shallower and, more to the point, 100-million-year-old and 180-million-year-old floor are no longer identical.

sections.name: Where things are
items: Eleven places were riding the wrong continent, and a new check now catches the whole class. A coordinate written down as an ancient position, which happens to land on modern ground, was silently attached to whatever continent sits there today.

All four of the great floodings of North America — the Sauk, Tippecanoe, Kaskaskia and Absaroka seas — were authored in the Caribbean and carried to 67° south, while the continent they flooded sat on the equator.

Laurentia, the ancient core of North America, was itself riding South America. The Catskill Delta was in Brazil, the Variscan mountains of France in the Sahara, the Caledonides in Western Sahara, the German Muschelkalk Sea in Libya, and the Sveconorwegian belt of Norway in Algeria. Each is now anchored on the place it is named after.

sections.name: The future
items: The continents assemble in the right places relative to one another. Australia had been welded to Africa's eastern edge; it is now a separate southern mass, and the average error in where each continent ends up fell from 38 degrees to 3.

Future collisions build mountains. Land above two kilometres was flat across the whole 250-million-year forecast — continents met and nothing rose. Now crust thickens where two masses meet, as it does at every collision in the past half of the model.

sections.name: New: Biotic interchanges
items: A sixth browsable panel, for what happened when two long-separated faunas finally met. It exists for the same reason the Climate events panel does: a land bridge is a few tens of kilometres wide, so the globe can show two continents approaching and never show the moment they touch — which is the only moment that matters.

The Great American Interchange, when the Isthmus of Panama joined two continents and North American mammals largely replaced South America's; the Trans-Arctic Interchange, the mirror image, when the Bering Strait flooded and about 300 Pacific species moved into the Atlantic; the Grande Coupure, when a falling sea level drained the Turgai Strait and 60% of Europe's mammal genera were replaced; and the Lystrosaurus Flood, when one animal spread from Antarctica to Russia across an empty Pangaea.
Each card says what opened the route, who crossed, who won, and what is still argued over.

sections.name: Life
items: Places that span sea and land show both again. A filter meant to stop oceans listing land animals was also being applied to the hand-catalogued lists, which hid organisms at 37 places. Solnhofen — a lagoon famous precisely for the pterosaurs and Archaeopteryx that fell into it — was showing neither, and continents in the Cambrian were being denied the trilobites that are the whole of their fossil record.

Ten more biogeographic provinces, and the Ordovician finally shows the ones it is famous for. The Ordovician has the most distinct regional faunas of any period in the early record, and it had been showing the fewest — because only labels that were themselves continents could reach the model. The Baltic and Mediterranean shelves appear, the Cambrian trilobite provinces appear, and so do the modern realms at the present day.

Cards say how big an animal was and what it ate. The illustrations have been ahead of the text for a while — a card could draw a creature accurately and never mention that it was two and a half metres long.
The Carboniferous rainforest collapse is marked as a Euramerican event everywhere it is mentioned. The Cathaysian rainforests of South China carried on to the end of the Permian.

The Devonian now gets less provincial as it goes on, which is what the record shows. Its three great marine realms were being held fixed across the whole period; the cold-water Malvinokaffric fauna of southern Gondwana actually disappears halfway through, and the Old World fauna spreads over most of what it and the Eastern Americas realm had held.

sections.name: Cards
items: The five disputed supercontinents now say what is actually disputed about them, instead of sharing one general sentence. Whether Pannotia ever assembled at all is a different kind of doubt from which ocean closes in each of the four rival forecasts of the next supercontinent.

The About panel now names the sea-level curve the model follows, and says that the rival published family puts the Cretaceous high stand at about half of it. It previously credited a curve the app does not use.

releases.title: The research release
releases.summary: Six rounds of background research had been deliberately kept out of the model. This release applies all of it: one reference frame for the whole map, real hotspots, a biogeographic province behind every card, and the shelf seas the Triassic was missing.

sections.name: Where things are
items: Every label, crater and volcanic province now travels on the same plate model the terrain is drawn from. Names sit on the ground they describe: features landing in the wrong ocean fell from 20% to 5%, and the number of labels that jumped impossibly far between two frames halved.
Fixed the Newark Rift Valleys, which sat in the Caribbean Sea, 3,300 km from the New Jersey basins they are named for.
Fixed the Cimmerian Belt, which was attached to a plate that never collided with Asia, so the mountains appeared without the collision that built them.
Retired the old reference-frame correction. With one frame there is nothing left to correct.

sections.name: The ocean floor
items: Hotspot chains are real places now. Hawaii, Louisville, Réunion, Iceland, the Galápagos, Kerguelen, Tristan da Cunha and 46 others sit at their true positions instead of being scattered at random.

Islands, atolls and flat-topped guyots now form a sequence along each chain as the sea floor cools and sinks beneath them. Midway reads as an atoll; the Emperor seamounts are drowned guyots two kilometres down.
Ten named submarine ridges added: Ninetyeast, the Emperors, Nazca, Cocos, Carnegie, Louisville, Chagos–Laccadive, Greenland–Iceland–Faroe, New England and Vitória–Trindade.
Volcanic islands can break the surface again. Iceland, the Azores, Cape Verde, Samoa, the Marquesas, St Helena and Réunion were all being held 1.3 km under water by a rule meant for procedural noise.
Fixed four dark, textured patches that appeared around every seamount and chain. They were submarine canyons being drawn on open abyssal plain, where there is no continental shelf to feed them.

sections.name: Land and sea
items: The Triassic and Jurassic have their shelf seas back. Ten named basins — the Muschelkalk, Zechstein, Sverdrup, West Siberian, Sundance, Russian Platform, Neuquén and the Alpine platforms — plus the broad continental shelf that ringed Pangaea.

The future no longer destroys a third of Earth's land. Continents were overlapping as they gathered into Pangaea Proxima, and the lower of the two was being deleted — which meant coastal plains and continental interiors vanished while mountains survived.
Pangaea Proxima is looser and assembles less abruptly, matching the published reconstruction it is based on.

sections.name: Climate
items: Raised the mid-Cretaceous to 33 °C. The previous curve peaked exactly on the boundary of its hottest category, so in 540 million years the world never once reached it.
Warmed the Palaeocene and Eocene, where carbon dioxide doubled but the temperature barely moved.
Lowered peak atmospheric oxygen from 36% to 30%, in line with the current review — and corrected the Guadalupian card, which quoted the old figure.

sections.name: Life
items: Click almost anywhere and the panel now names the biogeographic province that place sat in, at that age, with its characteristic plants and animals. 315 of 336 places get one; previously 235 of them showed the same worldwide list.
Mountain belts, basins, rifts, deserts and plateaus show life at all now. 133 places previously showed none.

Ten distinctive localities — Solnhofen, the Zechstein and Nama seas, the Muschelkalk, the Messinian salt basin, the Paratethys, Lake Pannon, the two mid-ocean-ridge vent faunas and the Beringian steppe-tundra — are flagged so the model never speaks over them.
Where the app can only offer the worldwide list, the heading now says so plainly instead of implying those animals lived at that spot.

sections.name: New: Climate events
items: A fifth browsable panel, alongside intervals, supercontinents, glaciations and extinctions. It carries the events that are shorter than the five-million-year spacing between frames and so can never be drawn on the globe.
Includes the Palaeocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum, the Azolla event, the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum, Oceanic Anoxic Events 1a and 2, the Hirnantian anoxia, and the Great Oxidation Event.
Added the Baykonurian glaciation, a terminal-Ediacaran ice age most compilations leave out.

sections.name: Cards
items: Four contested claims now say they are contested: giant arthropods and high oxygen, endemism after the Carboniferous rainforest collapse, and the closing of Panama.
Eduard Suess is credited alongside Wegener on the Glossopteris card. He used the same fossil evidence in 1885 and gave Gondwana its name.
New cards for the Permian Basin evaporites, back-arc basins, and Darwin's island-to-atoll-to-guyot sequence.
Large igneous provinces now name the ocean anoxic event or extinction each is the leading trigger for.
Plume cards now say that hotspots are not fixed, and that any track older than about 90 million years is a model output rather than a measurement.
The About panel now states, with numbers, what longitude is and is not: palaeolatitude is measured, but Palaeozoic longitude is a choice, and two published reconstructions differ by up to 146°.
Six new diagrams, drawn from the model's own tables so they cannot disagree with the map.

releases.title: The sea floor, measured
releases.summary: The ocean was rebuilt against real satellite imagery rather than tuned by eye, and a standing research programme was set up to check the model against the published record.

sections.name: The ocean floor
items: The deep ocean is one colour, shaded — not a rainbow ramp with depth. Below the sunlit zone nothing reflects off the floor, so all you see is the water column, and the old hue ramp was a mapping convention rather than an appearance.

Fixed a black speckle that outlined every continental margin, and pale blue-white flecks scattered across the open ocean — a sea surface was being lit by the shape of the sea floor kilometres beneath it.
Fixed concentric rings on every seamount, which turned out to be submarine canyons drawing the depth contours of a cone.
Abyssal hill provinces now change character across each fracture zone, as they do on a real chart, instead of running uniformly across the whole ocean.
Doubled the resolution of the elevation used everywhere, matching the source data exactly.

sections.name: Loading
items: The globe now appears in under half a second instead of eighteen. It fetches the frames it needs rather than all 1,506 up front, and re-aims as you scrub the timeline.

releases.title: The ocean rebuilt on the age of its crust
releases.summary: The sea floor stopped asking how far a point is from today's ridge and started asking how old the crust is — which is what actually determines its depth, its grain and its scars.

sections.name: The ocean floor
items: Basins now sit at the depth their crust has earned, from real surveyed crustal ages where the record survives and a model of past spreading where it does not.
Abyssal hills comb in straight parallel lines, as a real chart shows, instead of sweeping in arcs around the modern ridge.
Fracture zones persist across whole basins, because a scar travels with the crust it is cut into.
Abyssal plains appear with sharp edges where sediment has buried the hills. The Bengal and Indus Fans show up either side of India without being placed there.
Seamounts are a population of discrete volcanoes with real shapes and collapse scars, not a smeared streak — about 6,300 of them large enough for this map to hold.
The future ocean is no longer extrapolated from a plate model that has no data past its end.

releases.title: Ice, rivers and the deep sea floor

sections.name: Terrain
items: Rivers, marshes and delta plains derived from where water would actually flow across the reconstructed land, weighted by where the rain falls.
Drowned continents appear: Zealandia, the Kerguelen Plateau, Mauritia and the Seychelles rise and sink on their own schedules.
Fixed a burning, smeared north pole and the starburst that fanned out of both poles at high zoom.
Four times the rainfall detail, so large continents no longer come out in flat patches.

sections.name: Ice
items: The world had a quarter of the ice it should have had. Ice sheets now reach sea level and meet the sea ice beyond them.
The Cryogenian is two separate snowball glaciations with a real warm gap between them, not one long freeze.
Mountain glaciers respond to precipitation as well as temperature, so a cold dry range stays bare.

sections.name: Life
items: Fixed oceans showing land animals and every plate showing the same four species at a given age.
An African ape no longer appears on a card about North America.

releases.title: Lakes, labels that travel, and 273 illustrations

sections.name: Water
items: Lakes are derived from a water balance — rain in, evaporation out — so they fill and drain through time instead of being drawn on.
Present-day lakes use real surveyed outlines. The Great Lakes are only 14,000 years old and no longer sit in the Pliocene.
Inland seas that a 20 km grid cannot resolve, such as the Trans-Saharan Seaway, are seeded so their labels have water to sit on.

sections.name: Labels
items: Names ride their plate's real motion, so a feature keeps its label as it drifts instead of being snapped to whatever terrain is nearest.
Fixed interior features such as Lake Baikal snapping out to the ocean.
Labels are laid out to avoid overlapping, with a leader line where one has to move, and are dropped rather than drawn on top of another.

sections.name: Life
items: 273 traced silhouettes, so 45% of species draw themselves rather than showing a generic shape.
Mass-extinction cards, and an extinction-rate readout.
Region-specific marine life, ending the identical fauna in every ocean.

releases.title: Life through time, impacts, and the atmosphere

sections.name: New content
items: Browsable geological intervals and supercontinents, each with a summary and key events.
73 confirmed impact structures, each fading over its own lifetime — a marine crater is buried within a few million years while Manicouagan is still visible after 215.
Volcanic provinces persist as landforms for as long as they stood as high ground, rather than flashing for a single frame.
A climate-driven cloud layer, a day–night terminator, and river sediment plumes where big rivers meet the sea.
Solar brightening and a contracting biosphere in the deep future.
An About panel inside the viewer, and a full-screen ambient mode.

sections.name: Plates
items: Plate boundaries come from a real published rotation model resolved at every age, so boundaries and motion always agree with each other.
Plates merge going back in time — 49 today, about 8 in the Palaeozoic — instead of being re-invented at every frame.
Fixed a bug where any click within the last 25 million years selected a plate, making craters, eruptions and labels unreachable.

releases.title: First release
releases.summary: An interactive reconstruction of Earth's surface from 1,000 million years ago to 250 million years ahead, as a globe and an equal-area map.

items: 251 keyframes at five-million-year steps, built from published palaeo-elevation data.

The app ships physical fields rather than pictures, and assembles the world on your graphics card as you scrub — so coastlines genuinely migrate between frames instead of one image dissolving into another.
Climate is derived, not painted on: winds carry moisture inland and dry out, mountains cast rain shadows, and continental interiors go arid on their own.
Generated Precambrian continents, because nothing about a 900-million-year-old coastline is known well enough to trace.
